findings.title: Denial cache key omits identity type, so render:0 and anonymous:0 share deny entries
findings.body:
`userPermDenialCacheKey` is built from `checkReq.UserUID` only; the identity type is not part of the key. The renderer identity (`render:0`) and the anonymous identity (`anonymous:0`) both parse to UserUID "0", so they produce identical denial keys.

If anonymous is denied `dashboards:read` on dashboard X, that cached deny is then returned for the renderer's `dashboards:read` check on X, for up to 30s. The denial cache is consulted before `getRendererPermissions` runs, and that function grants `*` for reads. Rendering then fails even though the renderer is always supposed to be allowed. The reverse also happens: renderer denials poison anonymous checks.

Include the identity type (or the full subject) in the denial key.

findings.title: Un-invalidated denial cache short-circuits the new DB fallback and reintroduces the staleness the PR targets
findings.body:
The denial cache is checked before both the cached permissions and the DB requery. It is never invalidated when permissions change.

Any Check that is denied before a grant lands is answered `Allowed: false` for the full 30s TTL without consulting the DB. This includes a GET on a UID before the dashboard or folder is created, e.g. an import or uniqueness probe, a UI poll, or a request racing the creator's permission write.

The PR's stated goal is that a creator can immediately fetch what they just created. For any resource that was checked before its permission was written, the denial cache defeats exactly that, because the fallback to the DB is skipped.

Consider one of:
- not caching denials for specific names;
- keeping the denial TTL much shorter;
- invalidating or bypassing the denial entry when permissions or resources are written.

findings.title: Every new denied (name, folder) pair now forces a full permission DB query
findings.body:
`getUserPermissions` and `getAnonymousPermissions` no longer read `permCache`. On a cached deny, `Check` therefore always calls `getIdentityPermissions`, which runs `permissionStore.GetUserPermissions` against the DB.

Previously, all denials for a user and action were answered from the 30s permission cache. Now each distinct resource name (and parent folder) that a user lacks access to costs one DB permission query before its denial entry is written. Singleflight only dedups concurrent identical requests.

A restricted user, or a client issuing GETs for many arbitrary or non-existent names, turns each request into a DB query. This is a load amplification compared to before. The per-name keys also grow the local cache without bound within the TTL window.

Consider rate-limiting the refresh per user and action, e.g. refresh the permission set at most once per short interval, instead of once per denied resource.

findings.title: Ambiguous '_' delimiter in denial cache key causes collisions between different resources
findings.body:
The key is `namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent`. Dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores, so different (name, parent) pairs can map to the same key. For example, name="a_b" with parent="c" and name="a" with parent="b_c" both produce `..._a_b_c`.

A denial for one resource is then returned for an unrelated resource the user may actually have access to, for 30s. Use a delimiter that cannot appear in UIDs, or encode or length-prefix the components.

findings.title: Denial-cache test passes even without the denial cache
findings.body:
The test claims to "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but it seeds `permCache` with `{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`. `checkPermission` treats a false value as no permission.

The default `fakeStore` from `setupService` also returns no permissions, so the DB fallback denies too. The test would pass if the denial-cache lookup in `Check` were removed entirely.

To actually exercise the short-circuit:
- seed `true`, or configure the fake store to grant dash1;
- assert that the store was not called.

There is also no test that a DB-confirmed denial is written to `permDenialCache`, or that a subsequent Check skips the DB.
